title: A small SQLite store: one row per date, idempotent loads, monthly spreads

explain.prompt: In 3–5 sentences: why does the PRIMARY KEY plus INSERT OR REPLACE make loading the same file twice harmless? Why do you average a price (or a spread) over a month instead of summing it? What does the April 2020 Brent–WTI average tell you, and why should you be careful with it?
rubric: PRIMARY KEY (date) makes a second row for the same date impossible; INSERT OR REPLACE overwrites instead of appending, so re-running the load gives the same table (idempotent) — a plain INSERT would duplicate or fail.
A price is a level, not a flow: the natural monthly aggregates are the mean (average price paid over the month) or the last value, never the sum.
April 2020 averages a Brent–WTI spread of about 10 USD/bbl against roughly 3 USD/bbl in normal months: the storage glut and the negative expiry print dominate it.
One extreme day (a 55 USD/bbl spread on 20 April) adds about 2.4 USD/bbl to the monthly average (7.7 without it): report the median or the average excluding the event alongside it.
NaN is stored as NULL; the WHERE clause keeps only days with all three prices, so every month compares like with like (n_days shows how many).
